details:
**Madama Butterfly**
Puccini's opera set in Nagasaki, based on a John Luther Long short story (via David Belasco's play). U.S. Navy Lieutenant B. F. Pinkerton marries and abandons the young geisha Cio-Cio-San, who finally kills herself with her father's sword after learning he has an American wife. A motif from "The Star-Spangled Banner" accompanies Pinkerton.

**Tosca and Baron Scarpia**
Puccini's opera set in Rome in 1800. The singer Floria Tosca stabs the corrupt police chief Baron Scarpia after he promises to free her lover in exchange for her body; at the end she leaps to her death from the Castel Sant'Angelo. Scarpia joins the Te Deum at the end of Act I.

**La bohème (Rodolfo and Mimì)**
Puccini's opera about starving artists in Paris's Latin Quarter, based on Henri Murger's loosely plotted Scènes de la vie de bohème. The poet Rodolfo falls in love with the seamstress Mimì, who dies of tuberculosis (consumption) at the end, prompting Rodolfo's cries of her name. Jonathan Larson adapted it into the 1996 rock musical Rent.

**Mario Cavaradossi and "E lucevan le stelle"**
Cavaradossi is Tosca's lover, a painter. "E lucevan le stelle" ("And the stars were shining"), introduced by a melancholy B minor clarinet solo, is the tenor aria he sings while writing a farewell letter to Tosca as he awaits execution; the firing squad that was supposed to be using blanks actually kills him.

**Turandot and "Nessun dorma"**
Puccini's unfinished final opera, set in Peking (Beijing), about a cold Chinese princess who beheads suitors who fail to answer her three riddles. The "unknown prince" Calaf solves them and sings "Nessun dorma" ("None shall sleep"), ending with the triumphant cry "Vincerò!" ("I will win!"), wagering that she will not learn his name by dawn.

**"Un bel dì" ("One fine day")**
Cio-Cio-San's aria in Madama Butterfly, in which she imagines seeing a ship appear on the horizon carrying Pinkerton home to her.

**"Recondita armonia"**
Cavaradossi's Act I aria in Tosca. While painting a portrait of Mary Magdalene modeled on the blonde Marchesa Attavanti, he contrasts the model's beauty with that of the dark-haired Tosca, whom he loves.

**"Vissi d'arte" ("I lived for art")**
Tosca's Act II aria, sung after Scarpia demands that she sleep with him to save Cavaradossi. She asks God why she is being punished after a life of art, love, and piety (she even gave jewels for the Madonna's mantle).

**Gianni Schicchi and "O mio babbino caro"**
Puccini's one-act comic opera, the last part of his trilogy Il trittico (with Il tabarro and Suor Angelica). Relatives scheme to change the will of the dead Buoso Donati, who left his fortune to a monastery, and Lauretta sings "O mio babbino caro" ("Oh my dear papa"), threatening to throw herself into the Arno unless her father lets her marry Rinuccio.

**Ping, Pang, and Pong**
The three ministers in Turandot, who try to dissuade Calaf from striking the gong to enter the riddle contest and wistfully dream of their country homes, such as a house in Honan with a little blue lake.

**Liù and "Tu che di gel sei cinta"**
Liù is the slave girl in Turandot who secretly loves Calaf. In "Tu che di gel sei cinta" ("You who are girdled with ice") she tells Turandot that she too will come to love him, then kills herself rather than reveal his name; Calaf earlier sings "Non piangere, Liù" ("Do not cry, Liù").

**Franco Alfano and Toscanini**
Puccini died in 1924 before finishing Turandot, and Franco Alfano completed its final scene. At the 1926 premiere, conductor Arturo Toscanini stopped after Liù's death, telling the audience that this was where the maestro had laid down his pen.

**"Che gelida manina" and the lost key**
In Act I of La bohème, Mimì's candle goes out and she drops her key; Rodolfo and she search for it in the dark, and he takes her hand and sings "Che gelida manina" ("What a cold little hand"). Mimì later sings "Donde lieta uscì" when they part.

**Musetta's Waltz ("Quando m'en vo")**
The flirtatious waltz sung by Musetta in Act II of La bohème at the Café Momus to win back her former lover, the painter Marcello.

**Manon Lescaut and other operas**
Puccini's first big success, Manon Lescaut (1893), adapts Abbé Prévost's novel, also set by Massenet; it ends with Manon singing "Sola, perduta, abbandonata" as she dies in Des Grieux's arms in the Louisiana desert. His other operas include his debut Le Villi, La fanciulla del West (The Girl of the Golden West, in which Minnie loves the bandit Dick Johnson, actually Ramerrez), and La rondine.
